title: Classical Forms
intro: Most instrumental music from about 1700 to 1900 follows a handful of forms. Knowing them lets you hear where you are in a piece and what is coming next.

blocks.text: Two sections, each usually repeated (||: A :||: B :||). In rounded binary the opening material returns partway through B. In major keys, A typically modulates to the dominant and B returns to the tonic; in minor, A often moves to the relative major. Baroque dance movements (minuets, gigues, Bach's suites) are binary.

A statement, a contrasting middle section (different key, character or texture) and a return. Unlike rounded binary, the A section of ternary form is complete in itself, ending on the tonic. Minuet and trio movements (minuet–trio–minuet), da capo arias and many Romantic character pieces (Chopin's nocturnes) are ternary.

A refrain (A) that keeps returning in the tonic between contrasting episodes. Classical finales are often rondos. In the seven-part sonata rondo (ABACABA) the first B returns transposed to the tonic, as in a sonata recapitulation.

A theme, often a binary tune, followed by a series of variations that keep its harmony and phrase structure while changing the melody, rhythm, texture, mode or tempo. Mozart's 'Ah, vous dirai-je, maman' variations (K. 265, the 'Twinkle, Twinkle' tune) and Bach's Goldberg Variations, built on a bass line, are landmarks.
The most important form of the Classical era, used in first movements of sonatas, symphonies and string quartets. It is a drama of keys:

items: Exposition: first theme (primary theme) in the tonic; a transition that modulates; second theme in the dominant (or relative major in minor keys); a closing section confirming the new key. Usually repeated.
Development: themes are fragmented, sequenced and recombined while the music modulates through other keys. It ends with a retransition on the home dominant, building expectation of the return.
Recapitulation: the exposition returns, but the second theme comes back in the tonic, resolving the tonal conflict of the exposition.
Optional slow introduction before, and coda after.

blocks.text: Hepokoski and Darcy's Sonata Theory describes the exposition as aiming at an 'essential expositional closure' (the first PAC in the new key) and the recapitulation at 'essential structural closure' in the tonic; the medial caesura, a clear pause on V (or V of V) before the second theme, is a hallmark of the style.

Mozart's Piano Sonata in C major, K. 545, first movement, is the compact sonata form most pianists meet first: first theme in C (bars 1–4), a scale-run transition, second theme in G (bar 14), closing material, a short development starting in G minor, and a recapitulation that, unusually, begins in F major (the subdominant) so that the unchanged transition lands the second theme in C.

blocks.title: Which form
blocks.text: A piece goes: theme in C; new material in G; theme in C; new material in A minor; theme in C. Which form?
solution: A returning refrain in the tonic with different episodes between: A B A C A, a five-part rondo.

blocks.title: Sonata keys
blocks.text: In a sonata-form movement in D minor, in what key would you usually expect the second theme in the exposition and in the recapitulation?
solution: In minor-key sonatas the exposition's second theme is normally in the relative major, F major. In the recapitulation it returns in the tonic, usually D minor (sometimes D major).

blocks.text: Sources: Caplin, W. E. (1998). Classical Form. Oxford University Press; Hepokoski, J. & Darcy, W. (2006). Elements of Sonata Theory. Oxford University Press; Rosen, C. (1988).
